answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine line from Seneca’s Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 26 (“On Old Age and Death”). The Latin runs “Incertum est quo loco te mors exspectet; itaque tu illam omni loco exspecta”; the familiar English is Richard Mott Gummere’s Loeb translation, which reads exactly “You do not know where death awaits you; so be ready for it everywhere.”

source.excerpt: You are younger; but what does that matter? … You do not know where death awaits you; so be ready for it everywhere.
trail: The line closes Seneca’s Letter 26, “On Old Age and Death”, in R. M. Gummere’s Loeb translation.
Wikiquote lists it in its sourced section under Letter XXVI, crediting Gummere’s translation.
The Latin original — “Incertum est quo loco te mors exspectet; itaque tu illam omni loco exspecta” — is the ancestor of every English rendering.
Montaigne later quoted the same thought in “That to Philosophize Is to Learn to Die”, which is why it is often re-credited to him.
source.excerptNote: Gummere’s Loeb translation of the closing passage of Letter 26, where Seneca tells Lucilius that death keeps no reckoning of one’s age.
source.rightsNote: Seneca’s Latin has been in the public domain for centuries. The exact English wording here is Richard Mott Gummere’s translation, first published in the Loeb Classical Library’s Vol. I of the Epistles in 1917 — comfortably before 1931 — so this translation is public domain in the United States. A newer, in-copyright translation would render the line differently.

author.heading: About Seneca the Younger
author.metaLine: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman & dramatist
author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was a leading Stoic thinker, tragedian and adviser (later victim) of the emperor Nero. His Moral Letters to Lucilius — 124 essay-letters on how to live and die well — are among the most quoted works of Roman philosophy. Ordered by Nero to take his own life in AD 65, Seneca met the death he had so often written about.

misattribution.heading: The Montaigne mix-up
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Seneca is correct. The common confusion is a second credit: a paraphrased form is widely pinned on Michel de Montaigne.

items.scope: the popular ‘we / us / let us wait’ wording
items.why: Montaigne quoted the line in his essay “That to Philosophize Is to Learn to Die” (1580) — rendered in English as “It is uncertaine where death looks for us; let us expect her everie where.” Quote sites now circulate a smoothed version, “We do not know where death awaits us: so let us wait for it everywhere,” and credit it to Montaigne, though he was quoting Seneca.

misattribution.truthLine: Both belong to Seneca: the thought and the words are his, from Letter 26. Montaigne simply admired the line enough to borrow it.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Letter 26 is Seneca writing in old age, testing whether his mind has aged as fast as his body. His conclusion is the core Stoic exercise: because death can arrive at any moment and in any place, one should keep it constantly in view rather than fear its timing.

Montaigne, sixteen centuries later, built an entire essay around the same conviction — that to philosophize is to rehearse dying — and quoted Seneca’s line directly, which is how a Roman Stoic sentence ended up doubly attributed.
